findings.headline: National pay award of 3.3% exceeds budgeted provision of 2.5%, creating £1.2m pressure on contingency
findings.detail: The national local government pay award finalised in July 2026 at 3.3% is higher than the 2.5% provision made when setting the 2026/27 budget. This variance has not yet been reflected in individual service budgets and is creating a £1.2m pressure on the council's inflation contingency reserve. The contingency was set at £15.362m based on expected inflation of 2.8%.
findings.matters: An inflation contingency already containing only limited headroom above expected inflation is now reduced by an unfunded pay award, constraining the council's ability to manage other in-year price pressures.
findings.figures: 3.3% actual pay award vs 2.5% budgeted, £1.2m contingency pressure, contingency budget £15.362m
findings.quote: The national local government pay award has been finalised in July at a 3.3% increase. This is not yet reflected in service budgets and is higher than the provision (2.5%) allowed for when the budget was set leading to a pressure on the contingency of £1.2m.

findings.headline: Treasury position better than budget due to internal borrowing capability and higher investment income
findings.detail: Finance OSC shows a £0.688m underspend in Treasury. The budget assumed external borrowing would be required, but this has been confirmed as unnecessary — all borrowing needs can be met from internal resources, eliminating planned external interest payments. Additionally, interest earned on cash balances is expected to exceed budget due to elevated interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing capability is a significant strategic advantage for a council, reducing both cost of capital and refinancing risk; higher investment income improves the fiscal position.
findings.figures: £0.688m Treasury underspend forecast
findings.quote: the budget was set using the most prudent assumption around borrowing externally which it is confirmed can be met internally and hence no external interest payments are due. Due to global events, interest rates remain high and there is also a possible rate increase in year. Interest earned on cash balances is therefore expected to be higher than budgeted for.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecast surplus of £11.7m in year with closing balance of £152.658m
findings.detail: The HRA is performing significantly better than the general fund. The HRA is forecast to produce a £11.7m surplus in 2026/27 and a closing revenue balance of £152.658m. Overspends in repairs and maintenance (£2.9m) and supervision and management (£3.7m and £1.1m) are offset by slippage on external decorations (£5.8m), lower than anticipated depreciation (£1.8m), and rental income £1.8m above budget. This demonstrates robust rental income performance despite general fund pressures.
findings.matters: The HRA's strong reserve position and in-year surplus provides counterbalance to general fund pressures and demonstrates that the rental income base is performing robustly.
findings.figures: £11.7m surplus forecast, £152.658m closing balance, repairs overspend £2.9m, decorations slippage £5.8m
findings.quote: Overall, the most recent revenue forecast is showing an £11.7m surplus in year and a forecast closing revenue balance of £152.658m.

findings.headline: Waste disposal costs remain above budget despite substantial increase in recycling volumes
findings.detail: Environment OSC forecasts a near breakeven position, but this depends on £1.099m of mitigating actions. Waste & Recycling shows a pressure due to residual waste tonnages remaining above budget. The council's food waste collection rollout and recycling expansion were designed to shift waste to lower-cost disposal streams, but although recycling volumes have substantially increased, residual waste volumes remain high. Costs are being managed through grant-funded reserves.
findings.matters: A service expansion expected to generate savings through modal shift (waste to recycling) has not produced the anticipated benefit, indicating a gap between policy design and cost outcome that may affect future decisions.
findings.figures: £1.099m mitigating actions required for breakeven forecast
findings.quote: Whilst recycling volumes have substantially increased, the levels within the residual waste stream remains in excess of budget.

findings.headline: Children's social care overspend of £5.04m on placements and £1.9m on SEN transport amid growing complexity
findings.detail: Children's Services forecasts a £1.160m overall overspend, but within this, social care is forecasting a £5.04m overspend on residential and homecare provision for children looked after and children with disabilities. SEN transport is overspending by £1.9m due to continued growth in Education, Health and Care Plans and increasing complexity. These pressures are partially offset by utilising grant income (£3.56m). The forecast carries explicit risk that needs increase further, as has happened in previous years.
findings.matters: Placement and SEN transport pressures are widespread across councils; Wandsworth's specific forecast and explicit risk flagging shows the scale of the challenge and dependency on offsetting grant income.
findings.figures: £1.160m Children's overspend forecast, £5.04m social care placements, £1.9m SEN transport, £3.56m grant-funded offset, £3.179m mitigating actions required
findings.quote: Children's social care is forecasting a £5.04m overspend position. This is due to the costs of residential provision for Children Looked After continuing to rise as well as the increased cost of homecare packages for children with disabilities. There is also a £1.9m overspend forecast on SEN transport where there has been a continued increase in the number of children with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), alongside greater complexity of need.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation numbers grew 188 cases in Q1 to 5,005, with intake-to-move ratio currently 10 in for every 1 out
findings.detail: The number of people housed in temporary accommodation or owed statutory homelessness duty grew from 4,817 at the start of the year to 5,005 at Q1 end, a net growth of 188 cases. The council describes the current ratio as 10 people entering TA for every 1 person leaving. The paper states the council needs to stabilise numbers and achieve significant net reduction to bring the service back into budget. The forecast depends on fundamental reshaping of the practice model and changing the ratio to 3 in for every 10 out.
findings.matters: Growing demand for temporary accommodation is a material budget pressure; a council stating that demand is currently flowing in the wrong direction and that major service transformation is needed indicates a significant operational and financial risk.
findings.figures: 5,005 cases at Q1 end (up from 4,817), 188 net growth in Q1, current intake-to-move ratio 10:1, £4.6m mitigating actions required
findings.quote: Current overall numbers housed in TA or assessed as owed statutory homelessness duty as at the end of Q1 was 5,005 compared to a start of year position of 4,817, a growth of 188 cases. Currently 10 people come into temporary accommodation for every 1 that leaves.

findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £3.477m driven by unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need
findings.detail: Health OSC is forecasting an overspend of £3.477m, primarily in Adult Social Care. The paper attributes this to unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need, particularly in services for older people and adults with learning disabilities. The forecast includes £1.630m of future demand growth, of which £1.001m relates to children's care packages transitioning to Adult Social Care. Delivery of mitigating actions depends on assessments and reviews.
findings.matters: Unfunded demographic growth in social care is a structural pressure facing councils; quantified examples of the gap between statutory demand and available funding are material to credit assessments.
findings.figures: £3.477m Adult Social Care overspend, £1.630m future demand growth forecast, £1.001m from children transitioning to adult services, £0.608m mitigating actions planned
findings.quote: This position is primarily driven by Adult Social Care demand pressures, mainly relating to Services for Older People, Sensory and Physical Disabilities and Services for Adults with Learning Disabilities. This is reflecting underlying unfunded demographic growth and increasing complexity of need, particularly in services for older people and adults with learning disabilities.

findings.headline: General Fund projected to overspend by £5.306m at Q1 2026/27, dependent on £12m mitigating actions
findings.detail: The council is forecasting an overspend of £5.306m (1.7%) against a budget of £311.203m. This forecast assumes delivery of £12m of mitigating actions across services. The council had already added £16.9m to the budget when setting the 2026/27 position to recognise known service pressures, yet remains in deficit. If mitigating actions do not land, the overspend will increase.
findings.matters: A material forecast overspend that depends entirely on successful delivery of planned actions represents a significant risk to the council's in-year outturn and places pressure on reserves.
findings.figures: £5.306m overspend (1.7% of £311.203m budget), £12m mitigating actions assumed, £16.9m added to budget for known pressures
findings.quote: The Council is currently projecting an overspend of £5.306m (or 1.7%) compared to the approved General Fund revenue budget of £311.203m as at Q1. This forecast position assumes the in-year delivery of a total of £12m of mitigating actions.

findings.headline: Pension contribution rate reduced from 19.1% to 15.5% following improved fund valuation.
findings.detail: The Wandsworth Pension Fund's most recent actuarial valuation (31 March 2025) reported an overall funding level of 121%, improved from 116% at the previous valuation in 2022. Wandsworth Council's individual employer funding level improved from 131% to 135.9%. As a result, the overall employer contribution rate has reduced from 19.1% to 15.5% of pensionable pay for the three years from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2029.
findings.matters: This is a significant cost relief on the council's payroll during a period of severe financial pressure. The next valuation is due 31 March 2028, with revised rates taking effect 1 April 2029.
findings.figures: Funding level 121% (up from 116%); contribution rate 15.5% (down from 19.1%)
findings.quote: the overall employer contribution rate for the Council has reduced from 19.1% to 15.5% of pensionable pay for the three year period commencing 1 April 2026 and ending 31 March 2029

findings.headline: Pay inflation surprise: 3.3% award agreed against 2.5% budget, creating £1.2m ongoing overspend.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 national pay award for Council staff was agreed at 3.3%, whereas the budget had assumed 2.5%. This causes an immediate overspend pressure of £1.2m per year ongoing. The paper notes that increases in National Minimum Wage, London Living Wage and continuing impact of employers' national insurance contributions will continue to put above-inflation pressure on contractors' costs.
findings.matters: Shows the council's budget assumptions can be overtaken by external factors beyond its control. The 0.8% variance on pay creates £1.2m recurring cost. Contractor cost inflation continues to exceed general inflation.
findings.figures: 3.3% pay award versus 2.5% budgeted; £1.2m per year ongoing overspend
findings.quote: The 2026/27 pay award for Council staff has recently been agreed nationally at 3.3% whereas the budget assumed 2.5%, causing an immediate overspend pressure of £1.2m per year ongoing

findings.headline: Homelessness subsidy cap creating growing unfunded pressure as gap widens.
findings.detail: The Government's subsidy for Housing Benefit paid to households in temporary accommodation is limited to the Local Housing Allowance rate from January 2011, which has not kept pace with actual accommodation costs. As homelessness demand rises, households spend longer in temporary accommodation, and rents increase, the gap between what the council pays providers and what it can recover via subsidy grows. The council is taking action to manage demand through prevention, private rented sector discharge and out-of-borough placements, but these measures will take time to deliver.
findings.matters: This is a structural unfunded pressure that will persist and potentially grow if homelessness demand continues to rise. The council's recovery is limited by a fixed subsidy cap from 2011, while London rents have increased significantly since then.
findings.figures: Subsidy capped at January 2011 LHA levels
findings.quote: For housing benefit paid to households in temporary accommodation the Government's subsidy (reimbursement of the housing benefit paid out) back to councils is limited to the relevant Local Housing Allowance rate in January 2011

findings.headline: Children's social care overspend of £4m, driven by placement costs and SEND transport.
findings.detail: An overspend of £4m is projected in children's social care in 2025/26, despite Wandsworth's Children's Services being rated Outstanding by Ofsted in May 2026. Main pressures are rising complexity of need for children looked after and with disabilities, and transport costs from growth in SEND demand. The council is addressing this through early help and prevention, increasing local provision and improving placement commissioning, but these measures will take time to deliver.
findings.matters: Like adult social care, this is a demand-led budget where the council faces pressures from demographic and market factors beyond its control. A Good/Outstanding rating does not protect the budget from cost pressures.
findings.figures: £4m projected overspend
findings.quote: An overspend of £4m is currently being projected in this financial year

findings.headline: Adult social care overspend of £3.5m forecast despite service rated Good by CQC.
findings.detail: Wandsworth's adult social care is rated Good by the Care Quality Commission, but budgets are forecast to overspend by £3.5m in the current year. The paper attributes this to increasing demand, greater complexity of need and sustained care market pressures. The council is implementing initiatives including digital technology, integrated neighbourhood health and care, and strategic mental health commissioning to manage demand and improve efficiency.
findings.matters: Adult social care is one of the largest areas of council expenditure and remains a significant financial risk. Overspends persist even in a Good-rated service, suggesting demand and complexity are outstripping capacity and efficiency measures.
findings.figures: £3.5m projected overspend
findings.quote: budgets are forecast to overspend by £3.5m in the current year

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Budget deficit: Council to fund £3.3m plus potentially £6.7m more.
findings.detail: The DSB faces significant pressures from SEND overspends. The Government's High Needs Stability Grant will write off 90% of the accumulated deficit as at 31 March 2026 (approximately £30m for Wandsworth), but the Council must fund the remaining 10%, estimated at £3.3m. For future deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, Government support is unconfirmed; the council has estimated an additional £6.7m may need to be funded from General Fund reserves.
findings.matters: This represents an unfunded pressure on the General Fund from a demand-led, ringfenced budget. The council has limited control over SEND placement costs and demand. Additional £6.7m risk could materialise.
findings.figures: £3.3m (10% of accumulated deficit); £6.7m estimated for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits; accumulated deficit approximately £30m
findings.quote: The Council will therefore have to fund the remaining 10%, estimated to be £3.3m

findings.headline: HRA planned borrowing of £326m over four years to fund housing repairs and development.
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA), which manages 33,200 council housing properties on a ringfenced basis, is planning borrowing of £326m over the four-year framework period. This borrowing is needed to fund repairs and maintenance (including fire safety commitments and addressing stock condition survey issues) and investment in housing development and regeneration. The HRA revenue forecast shows a closing balance of £153m plus £25m of capital reserves.
findings.matters: This is significant new borrowing on top of the General Fund's financial pressures. For a lender, it shows the council's total borrowing trajectory and whether the HRA can service this new debt from rental income.
findings.figures: £326m HRA borrowing over four years; closing revenue balance £153m plus £25m capital reserves
findings.quote: an assumed level of borrowing of £326m over the four year framework period

findings.headline: General Fund borrowing reduced by £39m, avoiding £2.3m annual debt servicing costs.
findings.detail: The Spending Review has removed £39m of future General Fund borrowing from the planned capital programme, avoiding an estimated £2.3m of revenue debt servicing costs over four years. The capital programme has been reprioritised to focus on essential, affordable and deliverable schemes; lower priority schemes have been stopped, reduced or reshaped.
findings.matters: Shows the council is prioritising affordability by reducing new borrowing commitments and making hard choices about capital schemes. This protects the council's future revenue budget from long-term debt servicing costs.
findings.figures: £39m borrowing reduction; £2.3m revenue debt servicing cost saving over four years
findings.quote: The Spending Review has removed £39m of future General Fund borrowing, avoiding an estimated £2.3m of revenue debt servicing costs over the next four years

findings.headline: £79m of ongoing savings targeted by 2030/31, with significant delivery risk acknowledged.
findings.detail: The Spending Review identifies ambitious plans to deliver £79m of ongoing savings by 2030/31 across all areas of spending. These savings reduce but do not remove the budget gap. The paper acknowledges that delivery of savings at this scale carries significant risk and will require strong programme governance, clear accountability and regular monitoring. £29m of reserves has been allocated to fund the transformation investment needed (invest-to-save basis).
findings.matters: Savings of this scale are difficult to deliver and often slip. If not achieved on time or in full, the council will need to use more reserves or make difficult in-year cuts. For a lender, this represents a key delivery risk to the financial plan.
findings.figures: £79m ongoing savings by 2030/31; £29m reserve investment for transformation
findings.quote: Spending Review identifies ambitious plans to deliver £79m of ongoing savings by 2030/31

findings.headline: Reserves projected to decline to £76m—the minimum level needed to retain financial resilience.
findings.detail: Reserve balances have fallen from £205m in 2023 to £162m at the start of 2026/27 and are forecast to fall below £100m by year end. Current modelling indicates balances could reduce to around £76m by end of the MTFS period (2030/31), described as the minimum needed to maintain financial resilience. The council has allocated £29m of available reserves to a Spending Review Delivery Fund for invest-to-save initiatives.
findings.matters: A sharp reserve depletion reduces the council's financial buffer to absorb shocks. If reserves fall below £76m, the council would be financially exposed and unable to adjust to changes in circumstances. For a lender, this shows limited headroom for unexpected costs or if savings fail to materialise.
findings.figures: £205m (2023); £162m (start 2026/27); projected below £100m by end of year; £76m minimum by 2030/31; £29m allocated to Spending Review Delivery Fund
findings.quote: reserve balances have reduced from a high of £205m in 2023 to £162m at the start of 2026/27 and are projected to fall below £100m by the end of the year

findings.headline: Government grant funding loss of £84m per year by 2028/29—the largest cut in the country.
findings.detail: Under the Fair Funding Review and business rates reset implemented from 2026/27, Wandsworth is losing £19m in 2026/27 rising to £84m per year by 2028/29. This is a 40% cut in core government funding. Wandsworth was one of only six authorities nationally protected by the 95% funding guarantee (a 5% cash cut), while most boroughs received real-terms increases or full 100% protection. The loss reflects the formula treating Wandsworth as having low council tax and historically generous grant funding.
findings.matters: This structural funding gap cannot be closed by efficiency savings or service reductions alone. The council has identified it as the core driver of its financial crisis. For a lender, it shows the council's recurring income is being permanently reduced by an amount larger than many councils' total budgets.
findings.figures: £19m 2026/27; £84m per year by 2028/29; 40% cut; 95% funding guarantee (5% cash cut)
findings.quote: is set to lose £19m of funding in 2026/27 rising to £84m per year by 2028/29, a 40% cut

findings.headline: Council tax increase of 94% planned for 2027/28, from £510 to £1,468 Band D.
findings.detail: The paper assumes the council's share of Band D council tax will rise from £510 to £1,468 in 2027/28, a 94% increase on current year, with the total Band D bill (including GLA precept) reaching approximately £1,978. This large increase is made in a single year on the basis that phasing it over two years would run reserves down to unsustainably low levels. Council tax flexibility has been granted for two years; the decision will be taken by Full Council in March 2027.
findings.matters: This unprecedented increase shows the scale of the structural gap Wandsworth cannot close through savings alone and the revenue pressure it faces. For a lender, it signals political/collection risk if residents resist, and shows the council sees no alternative.
findings.figures: £510 to £1,468 (94% increase); indicative total Band D bill approximately £1,978
findings.quote: the Council should plan on the basis of its share of Band D council tax increasing from £510 to £1,468 in 2027/28

findings.headline: New income bands extend Council Tax Reduction support to additional low-income working households currently outside the scheme, caseload increase estimated at 50%.
findings.detail: The reform introduces new income bands for employed households to extend support to low-income workers who currently fall outside the scheme. The council projects this could increase WA4 and WA5 caseload by approximately 50%, though it explicitly notes 'it is not possible to accurately forecast the potential caseload increase'. The additional bands are intended to be permanent, avoiding cliff-edge effects as earnings rise and targeting support by ability to pay rather than benefit receipt.
findings.matters: Extends reach of subsidy with uncertain cost implications; peer councils assessing equity want to understand caseload impact; lender assesses whether additional demand brings scheme costs back up as savings plateau.
findings.figures: 50% estimated increase in WA4 and WA5 caseload (stated as estimate only)
findings.quote: It is not possible to accurately forecast the potential caseload increase and resultant costs of extending support through the creation of the new income bands. As an estimate, the modelling has assumed a prudent 50% increase in caseload to reflect the impact of additional bands for WA4 and WA5.

findings.headline: Proposed scheme changes identified as carrying risk of increased Council Tax arrears and demand for welfare and discretionary hardship support.
findings.detail: The paper acknowledges that reduction in CTR support may impact collection rates and result in increased demand for welfare and debt advice. The Equality Impact Needs Assessment identifies potential consequences including 'increased Council Tax arrears, recovery action, debt, requests for welfare or debt advice, and applications for discretionary or crisis support'. Option 3 was selected partly because it carries lower collection risk than the steeper Option 2, though risks remain.
findings.matters: Collection rate deterioration affects Council Tax income and may require additional recovery costs; discretionary support demand creates hidden budget pressure in social services; lender assesses whether true cost of reform offsets stated savings.
findings.figures: 7,102 households becoming liable to pay where currently liable to nothing; no quantified projection of arrears or collection impact provided
findings.quote: Any reduction in CTR support may impact on collection rates, levels of debt and result in increased demand for welfare, debt advice and discretionary support.

findings.headline: Working-age Council Tax Reduction scheme projected to cost £14.3m by 2030/31 if unchanged, against current spend of £6.9m, driving proposal to reform scheme.
findings.detail: The council has identified that maintaining current CTR support levels as Council Tax increases would become financially unsustainable. Under the do-nothing option, the scheme would cost £55.9m over four years, reaching £14.3m annually by 2030/31. The proposed reform (Option 3) is designed to stabilise the scheme at £7.1m by 2030/31 (total cost £40.8m over four years). The scheme currently represents just over 8% of total Council Tax income.
findings.matters: A finance director faces similar pressures from demand-led budgets; a lender needs visibility of whether the council can sustain its commitments; a peer council wants to know how others manage growth in CTR costs when Council Tax rises.
findings.figures: £6.9m (2026/27), £14.3m (2030/31 if unchanged), £12.5m (2027/28 reformed), £7.1m (2030/31 reformed), £55.9m (4-year cost do-nothing), £40.8m (4-year cost reformed), represents 8% of total Council Tax income
findings.quote: If Council Tax increases substantially, maintaining current levels of working age CTR discount would become financially unsustainable.

findings.headline: Council proposes £30.5m use of flexible capital receipts between 2026/27-2029/30 to fund Spending Review transformation costs
findings.detail: As part of comprehensive Spending Review, council intends to use central government's Flexible Use of Capital Receipts discretion to fund implementation costs including service redesign, IT infrastructure, and redundancy payments. Indicative annual budgets: £6.9m (2026/27), £12.6m (2027/28), £5.4m (2028/29), £5.6m (2029/30).
findings.matters: Revenue-support financing through capital receipts flexibility indicates revenue budget pressure; reliance on discretionary government mechanism rather than traditional funding; assumes capital receipts will be generated and government direction continues.
findings.quote: Spending Review Implementation 6.9 12.6 5.4 5.6 30.5

findings.headline: All usable capital receipts applied in 2025/26; council to rely on asset sales and discretionary financing for future years
findings.detail: Council states balance of available capital receipts was applied in full to 2025/26 expenditure, leaving no retained receipts. Future financing will depend on capital receipts generated from asset review and operational estate rationalisation, and use of government's Flexible Use of Capital Receipts discretion.
findings.matters: Depletion of receipts removes cash buffer; future capital and transformation financing dependent on successful asset sales execution and continuation of government discretion mechanisms.
findings.figures: Capital receipts contribution to 2026/27 programme: £3.3m (only 2.1% of total financing)
findings.quote: The balance of usable capital receipts held by the Council were applied in full to finance 2025/26 capital expenditure

findings.headline: 2025/26 capital spending underperformed by £27.7m (22.8%), with major schemes delayed
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure of £93.7m came in significantly below revised budget of £121.4m, a variance of £27.7m. Major slippages include Nine Elms Park (£10m delay due to external developer), Battersea River Wall stabilisation (£1.5m, technical complexity), and multiple leisure and transport schemes. Delivery challenges evident across the portfolio.
findings.matters: Persistent underspend indicates execution risk in capital delivery; suggests actual capital requirement may differ materially from forecast, affecting revenue impact and medium-term financial planning.
findings.figures: £121.4m budget, £93.7m actual spend, -£27.7m variance (22.8% underspend)
findings.quote: Total General Fund Capital Outturn 2025-26 121,423 93,746 -27,677

findings.headline: Council commits £3m in 2026/27 for Town Hall refurbishment design before finalising full business case
findings.detail: Administration has committed to refurbish Wandsworth Town Hall with £3m allocated for consultant appointment and RIBA design development. Paper states intention for scheme to be self-financing through capital receipts and revenue savings, but acknowledges full business case covering scope, costs, funding strategy, receipts expectations, and affordability "will be brought to Cabinet in due course."
findings.matters: Spending approved ahead of scope definition creates risk of cost overrun or requirement for additional funding beyond the £3m allocated; delivery depends on asset sale receipts still to be identified.
findings.figures: £3m for initial phase (2026/27)
findings.quote: £3m of capital budget will be set aside at this stage to fund this initial phase of the scheme

findings.headline: Despite reductions, council will need to borrow £112.9m over five years, with £52.4m required in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: Financing plan shows borrowing of £52.4m in 2026/27, £31.9m in 2027/28, £18.4m in 2028/29, and £10.1m in 2029/30, totalling £112.9m. This represents the council's significant ongoing financing need to fund capital investment.
findings.matters: Scale and phasing of borrowing affects debt service costs, prudential compliance, and council's financial resilience; front-loaded borrowing in 2026/27 concentrates refinancing risk.

findings.headline: Capital programme reduced from £350.3m to £313.2m; borrowing requirement cut by £33.7m through spending review
findings.detail: New administration's spending review removed or reduced uncommitted schemes worth £77.9m while adding £6.0m in new commitments. The net programme reduction of £37.1m lowers future revenue financing costs. Council states the changes reduce borrowing requirement by £33.7m.
findings.matters: Reduced borrowing requirement lowers future revenue pressure, directly improving medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £350.3m (previous programme), £313.2m (revised), £77.9m (reductions), £6.0m (additions), £33.7m (borrowing saving)
findings.quote: removal or reduction of uncommitted schemes totalling £77.9 million. Taken together with the application of available financing resources, these changes reduce the Council's borrowing requirement by £33.7 million, lessening the future revenue costs associated with financing the capital programme

findings.paper_title: Paper No 26-197 Pension Fund Annual Report 2025-26 - Appendix A PFAR
findings.headline: Pension strain costs nearly doubled year-on-year, indicating significant staff early retirements or redundancies
findings.detail: Strain costs (pension payments due to early retirement or redundancy) reached £2.2m vs £1.2m budgeted, with the report stating that 'The number of strain costs received this year was almost double last year.' This represents a material increase in unplanned staffing costs.
findings.matters: Increased strain costs reflect additional pension liabilities incurred through workforce restructuring; this signals the council has undertaken substantial staffing changes that may reflect financial pressures requiring deeper investigation against the council's budget and savings plans.
findings.figures: Strain costs £2.2m actual vs £1.2m budgeted (82% variance); number of strain cost cases nearly double prior year
findings.quote: Employers strain costs. Strain costs specific to the individuals being made redundant/retiring early. The number of strain costs received this year was almost double last year.

findings.paper_title: Paper No 26-195 Pension Fund External Audit Results Report - Appendix A ARR
findings.headline: Audit opinion remains provisional pending resolution of multiple valuation and disclosure issues
findings.detail: Ernst & Young cannot issue a final opinion until completion of outstanding procedures: resolution of valuation differences on two investments (Level 2 Schroders £3m and Level 3 unspecified), receipt of revised IAS 26 actuarial disclosures, completion of investment profit/loss work, and resolution of Currency Risk disclosure amendments. The report explicitly states work is 'subject to final review' on multiple material areas.
findings.matters: An unqualified audit opinion is the baseline expectation for fund administration; the number and nature of outstanding items indicate material issues remain unresolved as of the meeting date
findings.figures: 7 categories of work remain outstanding; 5 require joint EY and management action
findings.quote: Subject to completion of the remaining outstanding procedures outlined in this report, including executive review, we expect to issue an unqualified opinion. Please refer to Appendix B for Outstanding matters.

findings.paper_title: Paper No 26-195 Pension Fund External Audit Results Report - Appendix A ARR
findings.headline: Material prior-year disclosure error in Currency Risk note requires restatement of comparatives
findings.detail: The audit identified that Note 26 (Nature and Extent of Risks Arising from Financial Instruments) incorrectly included UK sterling denominated investments in the Currency Risk disclosure. Investments in sterling by definition carry no currency risk. This material error requires amendment of the current year and prior year comparative figures, indicating that financial statement review controls were inadequate in prior years.
findings.matters: Prior-year restatements reduce confidence in the reliability of the council's financial reporting controls; repeated disclosure errors indicate systemic issues in how the finance team prepares and reviews statements
findings.figures: Material issue requiring prior year adjustment
findings.quote: Our work on Note 26 Nature and Extent of Risks Arising from Financial Instruments is in progress, and has identified a material issue whereby the Currency Risk disclosure has included investments that are UK sterling denominated, and therefore do not have currency risk. This will also amend the prior year comparatives as a prior year adjustment.

findings.paper_title: Paper No 26-195 Pension Fund External Audit Results Report - Appendix A ARR
findings.headline: Incorrect cashflow data version submitted to pension fund actuary due to file-saving server issue
findings.detail: The pension fund submitted an older version of cashflow data to the actuary due to a file-saving issue on the server, resulting in the wrong version being used prior to completion of review checks. While the impact was limited to the IAS 26 actuarial disclosures, this indicates that controls over data management and third-party submissions lack adequate review and approval procedures.
findings.matters: Data quality failures in pension fund administration suggest control weaknesses in the council's finance function; poor controls over actuarial data could lead to understated or overstated pension liabilities
findings.figures: One incorrect data submission; classified as Low control deficiency
findings.quote: An incorrect version of the Fund cashflow data was submitted to the actuary due to a file-saving issue on the server. The impact was limited to the IAS 26 report, which forms the basis of the actuarial disclosures within the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Paper No 26-195 Pension Fund External Audit Results Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit complexity increased due to new team, regulatory requirements, and issues discovered during fieldwork
findings.detail: The new EY audit team for 2025/26 encountered more outstanding work than in recent years, partly attributable to increased audit requirements and partly to issues discovered during testing. The 2025/26 audit includes additional scope for the triennial valuation review, which is expected to lead to higher variation fees than the 2024/25 variation fee of £8,502.
findings.matters: Higher audit complexity and variation fees may indicate increased risk or control issues in pension fund accounting; audit team changes can affect consistency and depth of findings.
findings.figures: 2024/25 variation fee £8,502; 2025/26 expected to be higher due to triennial valuation review
findings.quote: There is slightly more work outstanding at this point than in recent years. This is partly due to increased audit requirements requiring more work to the same deadline, and partly due to the issues discovered during the audit work.

findings.paper_title: Paper No 26-195 Pension Fund External Audit Results Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Errors found in pension liability disclosure calculations given to the actuary
findings.detail: EY testing identified errors in how cashflow data was classified before being supplied to the actuary for IAS 26 pension obligation calculations. Although the overall position was correct, EY has asked the actuary to recalculate Note 28 to the accounts using updated data. Officers have added enhanced control procedures to prevent future errors in this complex calculation.
findings.matters: IAS 26 disclosures show the council's pension liabilities under accounting standards and are a key measure of long-term financial obligation; errors in how data flows to this calculation could misstate the reported pension liability in the accounts.
findings.figures: IAS 26 valuation errors identified; impacts Note 28 disclosure
findings.quote: EY testing found some errors in the detailed classification of the cashflow data (the total position was correct) given to the actuary to calculate the IAS 26 disclosures reported in Note 28 to the accounts.

findings.paper_title: Paper No 26-195 Pension Fund External Audit Results Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Two valuation differences discovered by auditors remain unadjusted above reporting threshold
findings.detail: EY found a £3m difference in Schroders fund valuation (below materiality but above the £1.6m reporting threshold) and an independent valuation difference for a private asset manager also above threshold. Officers do not anticipate amending the accounts for either difference. The Schroders issue involves a dispute over Northern Trust's valuation report, while private assets are noted as inherently subjective to value.
findings.matters: Pension fund asset valuations directly affect the council's reported financial position and future liability funding; unadjusted differences above reporting threshold suggest either auditor or manager valuation challenges that could understate the fund's true position or signal disputes with fund managers over asset values.
findings.figures: £3m Schroders difference; materiality £33.2m; reporting threshold £1.6m
findings.quote: EY are awaiting documentation from Schroders to support the valuation of their fund used by Northern Trust and reported in the accounts. The disputed value is around £3m and while this is well below materiality it is above the reporting threshold.

findings.paper_title: 26-178 Update on Accounts and External Audit 2025-26
findings.headline: Audit scale fees have increased 320% since 2021/22 and additional charges are expected
findings.detail: The PSAA scale fee for 2025/26 is £363,148, compared to £86,559 in 2021/22. Ernst & Young has advised that additional fees will be charged beyond this scale fee for work it considers additional. Additional fees for 2024/25 remain pending PSAA approval, with the council having paid only the scale fee so far, creating an uncertain future liability.
findings.matters: Rising audit costs represent a material ongoing claim on the council's finances that lenders need to understand when assessing the council's cash position.
findings.quote: The scale fee for 2025/26 is 320% more than the scale fee in 2021/22 (i.e. the last full audit pre the first disclaimed opinion). EY have indicated they expect to charge additional fees on top of this significant increase to reflect what they consider to be additional work on the audit of 2025/26.

Demand pressures particularly acute in social care, SEND and housing. Council established corporate Transformation Programme to achieve financial sustainability through service redesign and demand management.
findings.matters: Signals that MTFS savings targets may not be deliverable without proactive demand management action, raising execution risk around council's financial sustainability plans.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will reduce available funding with full impact phased from 2026/27 to 2028/29

findings.matters: Specific, material reduction in government funding over defined period creates structural pressure on financial sustainability and will require service efficiencies or reductions to maintain current spending.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued C3 judgment finding serious failings in Safety and Quality Standard
findings.detail: Wandsworth received C3 consumer judgment on 26 February 2025 citing serious failings and significant improvement needed. Ombudsman made 49 maladministration findings in 25 determinations with 82% related to repairs, complaints, damp and mould. Council established Housing Improvement and Transformation Plan and strengthened governance through Housing Improvement Board.
findings.matters: C3 judgment indicates significant control weaknesses in major service area with revenue and capital implications. Risk of undisclosed liabilities and further regulatory intervention.
findings.figures: 25 determinations with 49 maladministration findings; 82% of cases related to complaint handling, repairs, damp and mould
findings.quote: On 26 February 2025, the Regulator of Social Housing published a C3 consumer judgement for Wandsworth, concluding that there were serious failings and that significant improvement is needed, particularly in relation to the Safety and Quality Standard.

findings.headline: Building Control audit identified 2 Priority 1 findings
findings.detail: The Building Control audit resulted in 2 Priority 1 findings requiring immediate attention, alongside 6 Priority 2 and 2 Priority 3 findings. Building Control is a regulatory function, and Priority 1 findings indicate immediate compliance or safety risks.
findings.matters: Building Control deficiencies could indicate failures in regulatory oversight, safety compliance, or proper vetting of building work—all carrying legal and reputational risk.
findings.figures: 2 Priority 1 findings, 6 Priority 2, 2 Priority 3
findings.quote: Building Control Audit Final Reasonable Assurance 2 6 2

findings.headline: Internal audit function postponed or cancelled multiple planned audits due to resource constraints
findings.detail: Adult Social Care, Change and Innovation, and Resident Services each had planned audits cancelled or deferred to 2026/27 specifically because of 'limited resource availability'. Cancelled work included Homecare, Integrated Health and Social Care Services, Customer Service, and Out of Hours Emergency Services audits. The audit team prioritised higher-risk assignments instead.
findings.matters: Constrained audit capacity limits the council's ability to identify and remediate control weaknesses across operations. This weakens overall risk identification and governance. A finance director or lender depends on audit finding issues early.
findings.figures: At least 6 audits cancelled or deferred, affecting Adult Social Care, Change and Innovation, Resident Services directorates
findings.quote: limited resource availability, as noted above, with the remaining capacity prioritised to support audit assignments assessed as higher risk and more time-sensitive

findings.headline: Battersea Fields housing operation received Limited Assurance with 3 Priority 1 findings
findings.detail: The Battersea Fields RMO (Central Area), covering 512 units, received Limited Assurance from internal audit, indicating control deficiencies. It carried 3 Priority 1 findings (requiring immediate remediation), 13 Priority 2 findings, and 1 Priority 3 finding. Limited Assurance means auditors found significant control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Housing maintenance is typically a major asset and cost area for councils. Control weaknesses here could affect service quality, unit condition, tenant safety, budget execution, and asset stewardship.
findings.figures: 512 units, 3 Priority 1 findings, 13 Priority 2, 1 Priority 3
findings.quote: Battersea Fields RMO (Central Area - 512 units) Final Limited Assurance 3 13 1

findings.paper_title: Update on the Accounts and External Audit 2025-26 (Paper No. 26-178)
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.wandsworth.gov.uk/documents/s128001/26-178 Update on Accounts and External Audit 2025-26.pdf
findings.headline: Audit scale fees increased 320% from £86,559 (2021/22) to £363,148 (2025/26), with additional charges expected for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council's audit fees have escalated significantly. Additional fees of £118,536 have been requested for 2024/25 and are pending PSAA approval.
findings.matters: Audit fee escalation represents a material and recurring cost pressure on the council's budget; lenders need visibility on spending commitments and budget pressures.
findings.figures: Scale fee £86,559 (2021/22) to £363,148 (2025/26); additional fees £118,536 requested for 2024/25 pending PSAA approval; 2025/26 additional fees TBD
